title: The Break-Up
full_review:
Their tabloid-friendly romance notwithstanding, you may find yourself wondering how the characters played by Jennifer Aniston and Vince Vaughn in "The Break-Up" (Universal) ever got together in the first place.

The film is a tepid but only fitfully affable romantic comedy charting the deterioration of the relationship of art gallery assistant Brooke Meyers (Aniston) and loutish Chicago tour bus operator Gary Grobowski (Vaughn), who's in business with his brothers.

They meet cute -- though obnoxious is more like it -- at a baseball game where Gary makes a play for Brooke, who's sitting several seats away from him, by foisting a hot dog on her. He comes on way too strong, and his pickup lines are lame, but she falls for him anyway, and we see in the film's opening credit sequence (via still photos) how the courtship played out. A bit more detail of this period might have made their subsequent difficulties more plausible.

In any case, once the film proper begins, we find them sharing an impossibly posh condo (presumably Brooke comes from money, as neither could otherwise afford such opulence), and Brooke putting together a dinner party for their respective families, with Gary, the archetypal inconsiderate slob, merely wanting to unwind in front of a baseball game.

After a tense dinner, Brooke upbraids him for his self-centered ways, and more or less announces she wants out of the relationship. But as they both own the condo, the couple continues to cohabitate while sniping at each other, and each trying to get the upper hand.

Brooke tries to make Gary jealous by parading would-be suitors through the living room, and Gary moves into high gear to turn their apartment into a sloppy bachelor pad. Each receives questionable advice from his or her friends -- domestic guru Addie (Joey Lauren Adams) on Brooke's side, tough-talking bartender buddy Johnny O (Jon Favreau) in Gary's corner.

Gary's character is so patently inconsiderate and boorish, and Brooke's is so vulnerable and sincere, it's hard not to be rooting for her for almost the entire movie. You just know that Gary will become a more considerate person by the film's end, but the imbalance for the most of the movie is peculiarly off-kilter.

Director Peyton Reed draws good work from the stars -- especially the effortlessly appealing Aniston, who is so natural she hardly seems to be acting at all. Yet, her subtle telegraphing of every inner emotion is highly accomplished. Ann-Margret (in virtually a cameo role as Brooke's mom) and John Michael Higgins as her flamboyant brother add some variety, but it's scene-stealing Judy Davis as Brooke's queen-bee boss who gets the prize.

Refreshingly, there's no sex at all, though there are some brief flashes of partial nudity, including a fleeting strip-poker episode. The expletive and vulgarity quotients are fairly high, however, and along with the casualness of the premarital relationship, push the film into the "L" category.

Underneath the not-often-funny funny business, there are some universal truths about relationships, but the setup never quite rings true, as when at the eleventh hour, Brooke sweetly invites Gary to go with her to a rock concert they long ago planned, and he stands her up. Though his thoughtless behavior precipitates a revelatory moment for her, the situation is dramatically false. Overall, the script by Jeremy Garelick and Jay Lavender (with Vaughn sharing a story credit) could have been sharper, though to their credit, the film avoids a cliched denouement.

The film contains considerable profanity and crude language and an instance of rough language, some crass sexual banter, partial nudity and a permissive view of premarital relationship. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
